title: Page 213
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Defne her sabah vapurda aynı adamı görüyor: elinde kalın bir roman var, ama kitabın son sayfaları eksik. Defne ona söylemek istiyor, fakat çok utangaç ve adam cuma günü şehirden ayrılıyor.
paragraphs: Every morning at ten past eight, Defne took the ferry from Kadıköy to Eminönü. And every morning, the same man was sitting on the same bench, reading the same fat book.

Defne never spoke to him. She was too shy. But she watched him over her tea, and she watched his book, too. Every day, the pages on the left side of the book got thicker, and the pages on the right side got thinner. He was coming to the end.
She did not know his name. In her head, she called him the Book Man.
On Monday, the Book Man reached the last page. Defne held her tea and watched.
He turned the page. There was nothing. He turned back. He turned forward again. He shook the book, as if the missing pages could fall out. Then he looked at the sea and read in a loud, sad voice:
"'She opened the door, and she saw—' SAW WHAT?"
A woman with a baby moved to another bench. Defne put her hand over her mouth, because she wanted to laugh.

Then she remembered something. She worked at Blue Door Books, a small English bookshop near the ferry port. She knew that book. It was called The Lighthouse Letters, and she had read it twice. She knew exactly what the girl saw. It was the best last page in the world.
On Tuesday, she put a new copy in her bag. On the ferry, she sat opposite the Book Man. Her heart was going boom, boom, boom.
He looked up. His eyes went to her bag. Big white letters on the bag said BLUE DOOR BOOKS. He looked at the letters for a long time. Then he looked at Defne, and he smiled a small, strange smile.
Defne turned red and looked at the sea. She forgot all her words. When she found them again, the ferry was in Eminönü and he was gone.
On Wednesday, she was ready. She had three sentences in her head. She stood up, took a deep breath and walked to his bench.
At that moment, a seagull flew down, took the simit out of her hand and flew away.
"My simit!" shouted Defne.
The Book Man laughed. It was a warm, easy laugh. "Don't worry," he said. "Istanbul seagulls are professional thieves. One took my sandwich on my first day."
Defne laughed, too. Her three sentences were gone, so she said the only thing she could remember. "Your book stops on page 212, doesn't it?"
He stared at her. "How do you know?"
"I watched you on Monday. You shouted at the sea."
"I did," he said. "I'm Kofi."
"Defne. I work at a bookshop. We have that book. A complete copy."

Kofi's face lit up. "Really? Can you—" Then he stopped. "Wait. Tomorrow I have an early meeting. I take the seven o'clock ferry. And Friday is my last morning in Istanbul. My plane leaves on Friday night."
"Then Friday," said Defne. "I'll bring it."
"Same ferry," said Kofi. "Same bench."
On Thursday, the bench was empty. Defne told herself that this was normal. But all day at the shop, she watched the door.

On Friday, she arrived early. She had the book under her arm, in blue paper. At ten past eight, the bench was empty. At eleven past, it was still empty. The ferry's horn sounded and the boat began to move away from the port. Defne's stomach felt like a stone.
Then someone shouted, "Wait! WAIT!"
A man was running along the dock with his jacket open. He jumped onto the boat and stood there, breathing hard. It was Kofi.
"Sorry," he said. "My last morning. Everybody wanted to say goodbye."
Defne held out the package. He opened it carefully and turned to the end. His lips moved as he read the last page. When he looked up, Defne expected him to look happy. He looked worried.
"Defne," he said. "I have to tell you something terrible."
He put his hand inside his jacket and took out some folded pages. Eleven pages, with torn edges.
"These are the missing pages," he said. "They were in my pocket all the time. I tore them out on Sunday night."
"You did what?"
"My hands were shaking. It was an awful thing to do to a book."
"But why?"

"Because for three weeks, a woman in a green coat looked at me every morning, and she never said hello. And I never said hello, either. I was too afraid. So I thought: if the book is broken, she will have a reason to talk to me. Everybody wants to know how a story ends."
Defne stared at him. "I already knew how it ends! I've read it twice!"
"I know that now," said Kofi sadly. "It was not a perfect plan."
"It was a terrible plan. It took a week and a seagull."
"But it worked?" He smiled his small, strange smile.
Defne wanted to be angry. She really tried. But she was laughing too much.
"And on Monday?" she asked. "You shouted at the sea."
"Oh, that was real," said Kofi. "I felt very sorry for the book."
The ferry arrived at Eminönü. The passengers walked off. Nobody moved on the bench.
"I have to go to work," said Defne.
"My plane is tonight," said Kofi.
They looked at each other. The ferry was going to leave again in ten minutes.
Defne sat down next to him. He gave her the first page.
"'She opened the door, and she saw—'" she read. Her voice stopped working for a moment.
"Go on," said Kofi.
"'—him,'" she read. "'He was standing in the rain, smiling like a man who had waited a long time.'"
She looked up. Kofi was smiling his small, strange smile.
The ferry turned around, and neither of them got off. It was the first time in six years that Defne was late for work. She did not mind at all.

quiz.q: What is wrong with the Book Man's book?
quiz.explainTr: Kitap 212. sayfada, cümlenin ortasında bitiyor; son sayfalar eksik.
Martı Defne'nin elindeki simidi alıp uçar. Kofi buna gülerken ilk konuşmaları başlar.

quiz.q: Why did Kofi tear out the pages?
options: He was angry with the book.
He wanted a reason to talk to Defne.
He wanted to give them to the shop.
quiz.explainTr: Kofi, Defne ile konuşmak için bir bahane istiyordu; çok çekingendi.
Defne, vapur limanının yakınındaki Blue Door Books adlı küçük bir kitapçıda çalışıyor.
